newsitem.title: NEPAL: Communists seen braking Nepal's liberal drive.
newsitem.headline: Communists seen braking Nepal's liberal drive.

text.p: Nepal's drive for a more open economy may slow down now that a prime minister backed by communists has taken command of the Himalayan kingdom, analysts and business leaders said on Thursday.

Prime Minister Lokendra Bahadur Chand won a comfortable victory in a crucial vote of confidence on Wednesday with the support of the powerful Unified Marxist-Leninist (UML) party of former premier Manmohan Adhikary.
Chand promised a role for the private sector and said foreign investment would be welcomed in hydropower, where the mountainous nation has tremendous untapped potential.
"We will make efforts to strengthen the liberal and market-oriented economic system based on national interest," Chand told parliament on Wednesday.
But analysts said Chand may have trouble translating the promises into action.

"There may be questions raised in terms of operationalising them because political parties in the coalition stand for a certain ideology and have to convince their hard-core cadres," said Mohan Man Sainju, executive chairman of the Institute for Integrated Development Studies (IIDS), an economic think tank.
He was referring to the UML, which put the brakes on privatisation while it was in power for nine months following general elections in November 1994.
Business leaders said they were concerned that Nepal's free-market programme, launched in 1991, could be sidetracked by politics.
"Implementation of economic policies is always the weakness of Nepal," said Padma Jyoti, president of the Federation of the Nepalese Chamber of Commerce and Industry (FNCCI).
Nepal is among the world's 10 poorest countries, with 42 percent of its 21 million citizens living in poverty and lacking food, shelter, basic health care and education.
Four of five Nepalis are engaged in agriculture. They remain unemployed for most of the year as agriculture is seasonal and dependent on the annual monsoon.
The kingdom followed the lead of India, Nepal's biggest trading partner, when in 1991 it began opening up to trade and dismantling barriers to private investment.

The UML, the dominant partner in the coalition with 90 members in the 205-seat lower house, is under pressure from trade unions to protect jobs. It only reluctantly supports liberal economic policies.
Chand's faction of the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP) has only 10 legislative seats.

The new prime minister is under pressure from the communists to conduct early local elections to 4,000 village and 50 municipal authorities throughout the country. The polls were delayed by the outgoing centrist government.
Analysts said local polls were seen as crucial popular test-runs of the parliamentary polls that the communists want to hold earlier than scheduled in late 1999.
"If the government does not hold local elections immediately we will oppose it," said Pradeep Nepal, a central committee member of the UML.
